summary: NVIDIA Cosmos is a family of world models for what NVIDIA calls physical AI: robots, vehicles and machines that act in the real world. The current family, Cosmos 3, was published on 31 May 2026 under the Linux Foundation's OpenMDW-1.1 licence, with open weights in three sizes and a training and serving framework beside them. It has two faces. One reads pictures and video and writes text, answering questions about what is happening, when it happened and where in the frame it is. The other generates: given a text prompt, a starting image, a video or a stream of actions, it produces images, video, sound muxed into the video, and action trajectories for a named robot or vehicle, including the future a given action would bring about and the actions that would bring about a given future. Scored against this map it is almost entirely out of scope, and that is the finding rather than a gap in the research: sixty-four of the eighty-nine rows describe machinery Cosmos does not have, because it has no scene, no objects, no transforms, no materials, no lights and no physics engine, and its own limitation notice says so, stating that the model lacks an explicit physics simulator and that geometry, object permanence and contact dynamics are only approximated. What it does have that this map can see is narrow and worth naming: a camera it can be driven by and can estimate, in nine numbers a frame; a time-sampled action record; scene text as a measured concern; and a guardrail on generation. Four things a standards audience should carry away. The only structured description of a scene in the whole platform is the JSON prompt handed to the generator, and every field in it is prose, so the interchange artefact of a world model is a paragraph in slots. The action trajectory, which is the one numeric record Cosmos both reads and writes, cannot be read by anything else: its columns mean whatever the named embodiment says they mean, its values are normalised by figures taken from the training set, and decoding them needs a projection matrix that lives inside the model. Nothing marks a Cosmos output as generated, though a safety classifier and a face blur do run over the frames. And nothing anywhere expresses a position on the Earth, in a platform trained on ten thousand hours of driving. Two traps for anyone planning on this. The autoencoder in the generation path is not NVIDIA's: it is taken from the Wan2.2 model, published by Wan-AI under Apache 2.0, and kept frozen, so a separately owned component sits inside what an OpenMDW notice appears to cover. And the platform's own publications already contradict each other: the documentation site still gives Apache 2.0 and the NVIDIA Open Model License where the repository, the model card and the technical report all give OpenMDW-1.1, and says the guardrail cannot be disabled where the shipped code documents four ways to disable it.

coverage.note: Nothing is rasterised, because there is no geometry to rasterise. Pixels are produced by denoising latent tokens and decoding them through a video autoencoder, and that autoencoder is not NVIDIA's own: the generation encoder is taken from the Wan2.2 model, published by Wan-AI under Apache 2.0, and is frozen during training. There is no render pass, no draw call and no render graph anywhere in the platform.
